title: Quadruped Oil Lamp

image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A small glazed clay oil lamp shaped like a four-legged animal, shown against a plain background.

context: A small oil lamp of glazed earthenware, attributed to Egypt and dated to the 11th to 12th century. The title describes it as a quadruped, meaning a four-footed animal form. It is only about 9 centimeters long. In the 11th century Egypt was ruled by the Fatimid dynasty, and lamps like this burned oil to give light.

descriptions.k: This is a little lamp made of clay. It is shaped like an animal with four legs. People in Egypt used it to make light a very long time ago. It is about as long as your hand. What animal could it be?
descriptions.g12: This tiny lamp was made in Egypt almost a thousand years ago. It is shaped like an animal with four legs. People put oil inside it to make light. It is made of clay with a shiny coating called a glaze. Why would someone make a lamp look like an animal?
descriptions.g35: This small lamp was made in Egypt about a thousand years ago. It is shaped like a four-legged animal, and it is only about 9 centimeters long. The maker shaped clay, added details, and covered it with a glaze, a glassy coating. People burned oil in lamps like this for light. Look at the shape. Why might the maker turn an everyday object into an animal?
descriptions.g68: Oil lamps were everyday objects in medieval Egypt, but this one has been shaped into a four-footed animal. The museum lists applied, incised, and cut decoration plus glaze, which means the maker added pieces of clay, scratched lines, and cut details before coating it. At about 9 centimeters long, it is small enough to hold in a hand. The record does not say what animal it shows, so we can look for clues. How does making a useful object playful change how people might notice it?
descriptions.g910: This glazed earthenware lamp, attributed to Egypt in the 11th to 12th century, shows how everyday ceramics could carry sculpture. The maker built an animal form, added features with applied clay, incised lines, and cut openings, then glazed the surface. Animal-shaped vessels were made in many parts of the medieval Islamic world. The record names it only as a quadruped, so the specific animal remains uncertain. How do function and playfulness coexist in this small object?
descriptions.g1112: This small lamp fuses utility and sculpture. Its quadruped form, built with applied, incised, and cut details under a glaze, reflects a ceramic tradition in medieval Egypt that valued skilled surface work even in everyday objects. The museum record does not specify which animal is represented or how the lamp was used in a home, so claims about symbolism should be tentative. How can we treat common objects as evidence of ordinary life without reducing them to simple tools?

teacherNote.context: A small glazed earthenware oil lamp attributed to Egypt, 11th to 12th century. The record does not say which animal is shown or how it was used, so treat both as open questions.
directions: Have students shape a small animal from clay or play dough and add one scratched (incised) detail.
Compare this lamp to a modern lamp: what stayed the same about the need for light, and what has changed?
Ask students to choose another everyday object and imagine how a maker could make it playful without losing its function.
